title: operator-taxonomy-and-g2m-hooks-selfhost-inference
content:
Objective:
Provide a practical operator-first taxonomy of the operational gaps buyers hit when they choose vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM style self-hosted stacks, and surface concise GTM messaging and SE playbook items that close the build-vs-buy conversation. This doc is written for GTM, sales engineering, and product marketing to quickly reference tradeoffs and craft tailored rebuttals and POC success criteria.

Thesis (1-line):
Many engineering teams choose self-hosted inference to control cost and data locality, but they underestimate the ongoing operator complexity required to keep SLOs, quality, and unit economics stable at scale; Redwood’s value is operationalizing those invisible costs while preserving control.

Buyer personas and primary goals: (quick notes)
- Startup ML infra lead (50–200 devs): wants low per-token cost, fast iteration, but limited ops headcount. Concern: time-to-MVP and rework.
- Platform/AI infrastructure at scale (enterprise): needs predictable latency/SLOs, isolation, compliance, and central observability. Concern: long-term maintenance & auditability.
- Product engineer building feature (single-team): wants simple API, streaming, and predictable debugging when hallucinations/regressions appear. Concern: day-to-day DX.

Operational taxonomy — where self-hosted spikes cost/risk (with short concrete symptoms):
1) Model build/format compatibility
   - Symptoms: different model checkpoints require conversion steps, quantization scripts fail on edge cases, TRT plugins missing.
   - Hidden cost: repeated engineering time for conversion, debugging kernel failures, maintaining container variants.
2) Latency tail and batching behavior
   - Symptoms: fluctuating p50/p95 when traffic mixes sync and streaming requests; naive batching increases tail latency.
   - Hidden cost: complex batching heuristics and per-service tuning.
3) Memory fragmentation and KV cache handling
   - Symptoms: OOMs under long-context workloads; cold-start penalty when KV cache not warmed.
   - Hidden cost: engineering time to implement persistent cache, cache warm strategies, and eviction policies.
4) Multi-GPU sharding and interconnect inefficiencies
   - Symptoms: sublinear scaling when adding GPUs, network bottlenecks for tensor+pipeline parallel setups.
   - Hidden cost: ops time to tune TP/PP configs and manage node-level degradations.
5) Quantization and kernel correctness
   - Symptoms: quality regressions with INT8 or custom quant formats; accuracy vs perf tradeoffs unclear.
   - Hidden cost: repeated eval runs, dataset drift monitoring, guardrails to rollback.
6) Observability and debugging
   - Symptoms: limited token-level tracing, poor correlation between model versions and downstream errors.
   - Hidden cost: bespoke traces, manual annotations, long SE cycles to root cause regressions.
7) Upgrades, rollouts, and fallback policies
   - Symptoms: risky model upgrades cause outages; no consistent canary/A-B deployment tooling; fallback to smaller model manual.
   - Hidden cost: dedicated release windows and runbooks.
8) Security/compliance and secret management
   - Symptoms: ad-hoc KMS integration, unclear audit trails for model access.
   - Hidden cost: engineering/legal time to validate and instrument.

Comparative snapshot: vLLM vs TGI vs TensorRT-LLM (operational dimensions) — high level qualitative notes
- vLLM (open-source optimized runtime):
  - Strengths: agile for researchers, good for experimenting with KV cache strategies and early batching logic.
  - Weaknesses: patchwork support for enterprise-grade autoscaling, operator must implement tracing, model upgrade logic, and broad model-format compatibility.
  - Typical pain: multi-tenant isolation and predictable p95 at production scale.
- TGI (NVIDIA Text Generation Inference):
  - Strengths: optimized kernels, TensorRT integrations, good perf on NVIDIA stack, strong quantization support.
  - Weaknesses: limited out-of-the-box rollout/observability primitives, dependency on Triton ecosystem and occasional plugin fragility.
  - Typical pain: portability across cloud/hardware and non-NVIDIA infra.
- TensorRT-LLM / custom TRT stacks:
  - Strengths: best-in-class latency/cost for int8/fp16 if everything compiles and plugins exist.
  - Weaknesses: high engineering overhead to maintain build pipelines and ensure correctness across model revisions; brittle to model architecture changes.
  - Typical pain: conversion regressions, hard-to-debug numerical edge cases.

Where managed inference (Redwood hosted/dedicated/private) systematically reduces ops friction
- Unified runtime with pre-built conversions and model variants reduces conversion burden.
- Built-in continuous batching + adaptive latency policies reduce p95 tails without manual heuristics.
- Prefix/KV caching integrated into serving layer (warmed and persisted) reduces cold token costs.
- Out-of-the-box rollouts (canary, A/B, automatic fallback) reduce upgrade risk.
- Token-level observability and cost attribution cut SE time in half for triage.
- Enterprise controls (VPC, KMS, audit logs) without building plumbing.

GTM messaging snippets (short, role-targeted)
- For platform/infrastructure leads: "Keep control of models and data without inheriting a full-time ops team. We’ll own the runtime complexities — you keep the SLA and cost levers."
- For product engineers: "Same API in dev and prod — no surprises when you scale. Streaming, function-calls, and predictable latency out of the box."
- For procurement/compliance: "Private deployments with KMS and audit trails — skip the multi-quarter compliance project."

Common objections and concise rebuttals (SE-friendly)
- "We can build this ourselves cheaper." -> "Initial infra might cost less on paper, but recurring costs show up in perf regressions, outrun debugging, and lost developer cycles; we can run a quick cost-per-token + SRE-effort baseline during the POC."
- "We need full control over model builds." -> "You retain model ownership and version pinning; our runtime supports private model registries and custom variants — we only remove the labor of maintaining conversions and kernels."
- "Our infra is GPU-heavy and proprietary." -> "Redwood supports dedicated/private deployments with the same operational primitives; we integrate with on-prem GPUs and respect interconnect/topology constraints while bringing rollout and observability."

SE POC checklist and success criteria (recommended minimal scope for a convincing POC)
1) Baseline perf test: run identical workload on customer self-hosted stack (vLLM/TGI/TRT) and Redwood dedicated/hosted. Measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost-per-token over a 48–72 hour mixed workload.
2) Failure injection: simulate node OOM, model conversion failure, and rolling upgrade to verify automatic fallback.
3) Quality regression check: deploy a new quantized variant and measure eval prompt-set pass rate and downstream metric delta.
4) Observability demo: reproduce a query-level debug session showing token-level timing, model version, and cost attribution.
5) Compliance demo (if required): show KMS key rotation, access logs, and VPC isolation steps.
POC success = matched or better p95 with lower SE burden + clear path to predictable cost.

Pricing and negotiation levers to highlight to customers
- Show unit economics: per-token delta vs estimated ops FTE time for 6–12 months.
- Highlight predictable reserved capacity for enterprises to stabilize spend.
- Offer a limited-time migration credit for migration engineering and conversion support.

Suggested collateral and content pieces to support this motion
- A short technical appendix (2–3 pages) comparing failure modes across vLLM/TGI/TRT with trace examples.
- A one-pager CTO checklist: "What you actually solve when you buy managed inference."
- Recorded demo: canary rollout + automatic fallback + token-level tracing teardown.

Open questions / follow-ups for product: (to convert into backlog)
- Can we publish a reproducible benchmark that isolates impact of KV cache warm strategies across typical enterprise prompt patterns?
- What minimum feature set for private deployments closes 80% of enterprise objections (KMS, audit logs, VPC, model pinning)?
- Investigate a guided conversion utility that maps common model formats to Redwood-verified variants and flags risky ops (unsupported plugins, op-level numeric instability).

Next steps for GTM / SE team:
1) Convert these talking points into a 1-page cheat sheet for sales and a demo playbook for SEs.
2) Prioritize collateral: benchmark appendix + CTO checklist + recorded SE demo.
3) Schedule two joint customer Q/A sessions where we run the POC checklist live.

Notes to self (informal):
- Capture a short list of the top 5 real customer war stories about self-hosted surprises — very convincing for procurement.
- Make sure bench infra uses identical CUDA/cuDNN/TensorRT versions when comparing to avoid false negatives.

References / inspiration: internal bench PR, large-customer notes, and public docs from vLLM/TGI/TensorRT.
